The observed filament properties indicate gas processed in the cluster environment and influenced by the infalling group, and comparisons with SLOW confirm qualitatively consistent behavior with an actively accreting cluster in the cosmic web.

title: Invariant manifolds in barred galaxy simulations. III. Self-regulated weakening of strong spiral arms
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in A&A on 30/07/2026
summary: We investigated the origin of the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies, seeking the physical mechanism responsible for the decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles over time. We reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body simulation of a barred galaxy using AGAMA, computed the Lagrangian points, and quantified how their spiral-induced angular displacement affects the geometry of the invariant manifolds and the associated orbital flows. We find that sufficiently strong, self-gravitating spiral arms significantly reshape the gravitational potential of a barred galaxy, displacing the equilibrium points up to 20-50° from the bar major axis, where they are expected to lie in the standard invariant-manifold framework. This shift alters the configuration of the manifold branches and disrupts the coherent stellar flows that sustain the spiral structure. As the spiral weakens, the equilibrium points gradually return to their standard configuration, restoring the conditions for manifold-driven spiral arm formation on a timescale of ~200 Gyr. We show for the first time that invariant manifolds and the spiral structures they generate are coupled through a self-regulating feedback mechanism, allowing the spiral pattern to recur over time. Our results therefore indicate that, although barred galaxies may sustain spiral activity over long timescales, individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why strong spiral arms in barred galaxies weaken over time. Using AGAMA to reconstruct the potential of an N-body simulation, the authors show that strong self-gravitating spirals displace Lagrangian points by 20-50° from the bar axis, disrupting invariant manifolds and coherent stellar flows. As spirals weaken, equilibrium points return to standard positions over ~200 Gyr, restoring manifold-driven spiral formation. This reveals a self-regulating feedback loop between manifolds and spirals, making individual spiral episodes transient despite long-term spiral activity.
AI.motivation: To identify the physical mechanism behind the observed decline in the fraction of manifold-trapped particles and the weakening of strong spiral arms in barred galaxies.
AI.method: Reconstructed the gravitational potential of a fully self-consistent N-body barred galaxy simulation using AGAMA; computed Lagrangian points; quantified how spiral-induced angular displacement of equilibrium points affects invariant manifold geometry and associated stellar orbital flows.
AI.result: Strong self-gravitating spiral arms displace equilibrium points by 20-50° from the bar major axis, altering manifold branch configuration, disrupting coherent stellar flows, and weakening the spiral. Equilibrium points return to standard positions over ~200 Gyr as spirals weaken, restoring manifold-driven spiral formation. This is the first demonstration of a self-regulating feedback mechanism coupling invariant manifolds and spiral structures.
AI.conclusion: Barred galaxies can sustain spiral activity over long timescales through a self-regulating feedback mechanism, but individual episodes of strong spiral arms are intrinsically transient.

title: Domain walls through different cosmologies
comment: 30 pages, 8 figures
summary: We study properties of domain walls (DWs) arising in the model with a double well potential assuming different early universe cosmologies: from dust through stiff matter domination to the limit of effective Minkowski space. Using lattice simulations we demonstrate that evolution of DW networks exhibits an approximate universality with respect to the cosmological equation of state (EoS). Namely, the wall area inside a given large volume is mainly determined by the particle horizon, while details of cosmic expansion play a subdominant role. As it follows, particle horizon rather than the inverse Hubble rate is pivotal in DW evolution defining the network correlation length and hence its phenomenology, e.g., the characteristic wavelength of emitted gravitational waves (GWs). Formation of closed DWs is shown to be very sensitive to the cosmological EoS and hence violate the universality, but their contribution to the total network is too small to change the overall picture. The universality breaking is also observed in the spectral properties of GWs from annihilating (biased) DWs: i) the IR slope of the spectrum depends on the EoS parameter; ii) there is a plateau in the UV part of the spectrum, which gets more pronounced as one stiffens the EoS. However, the dependence on the EoS is rather weak in the near peak region, which is most relevant from the viewpoint of pulsar timing arrays and other searches for the stochastic GW background. For a selection of primordial cosmologies, we provide fitting formulae for the spectra near the peak.

AI.tldr: The paper studies domain wall (DW) network evolution in models with a double well potential across different early universe cosmologies (dust, stiff matter, Minkowski limit). Using lattice simulations, it finds approximate universality of DW evolution with respect to the cosmological equation of state (EoS): the particle horizon (rather than the inverse Hubble rate) primarily governs the wall area and network correlation length, and hence the characteristic GW wavelength. Closed DW formation is EoS-sensitive but contributes negligibly. Spectra of GWs from annihilating DWs show EoS-dependent IR slopes and increasingly pronounced UV plateaus for stiffer EoS, though near-peak behavior is largely EoS-independent. Fitting formulae near the peak are provided for a selection of primordial cosmologies.
AI.motivation: To understand how domain wall network evolution and their gravitational wave signatures depend on the cosmological equation of state in different early universe scenarios, particularly to identify which quantities (particle horizon vs. Hubble rate) are pivotal and whether universality holds across different cosmologies.
AI.method: Lattice (numerical) simulations of domain wall networks in a double well potential, scanning across cosmological expansion histories from dust to stiff matter domination and the Minkowski limit, analyzing DW network properties (area, correlation length), closed wall formation, and gravitational wave spectra from biased (annihilating) DWs.
AI.result: (i) DW network evolution shows approximate universality w.r.t. EoS—wall area is governed primarily by the particle horizon, not the inverse Hubble rate. (ii) Closed DW formation violates this universality but contributes negligibly to the total network. (iii) GW spectra from annihilating DWs show EoS dependence in the IR slope and a UV plateau that becomes more pronounced for stiffer EoS; near-peak behavior is weakly EoS-dependent. Fitting formulae for peak spectra are provided.
AI.conclusion: The particle horizon (not the Hubble rate) is the key scale governing DW network evolution and phenomenology. Although some EoS-dependent effects (closed-wall formation, IR/UV spectral features) exist, the near-peak GW signal—most relevant for pulsar timing arrays—is largely universal across cosmologies, permitting simplified modeling and fitting formulae for observational predictions.

title: A search for HI absorption in distant star-forming galaxies with ASKAP-FLASH - II. Direct observations and stacking of 21 cm line
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present results of a search for associated and intervening HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies and a control sample of radio galaxies at 0.4 < $z$ < 1.0, using ASKAP's FLASH HI 21 cm absorption survey. We report the detection of a new HI 21 cm absorption line in radio galaxy NVSS J214954-004657 at $z_{\mathrm{HI}}$ = 0.863. Additionally, we present results of HI 21 cm stacking for associated and intervening star-forming and radio galaxy catalogues. For the first time at these redshifts, we report tentative detections of stacked HI 21 cm absorption for associated galaxies when stacked in order of descending radio source brightness, and show that these tentative detections become buried as optical depth increases as progressively weaker sources are co-added into the stack. No stacked signal is detected when co-adding intervening galaxy spectra. We speculate that the ability to detect a stacked HI 21 cm detection is dependent on the background source optical depth limits, as well as source covering factors. Covering factor has a greater impact when stacking intervening systems, and can be considered to effectively weaken the observed flux density of a radio source. We find no significant difference in detection rate for associated HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming galaxies versus the general radio-source population at the same redshift. Although detection rates are low, from a meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys we find that 1 detection is expected given the survey parameters.

AI.tldr: A search for HI 21 cm absorption in star-forming and radio galaxies at 0.4<z<1.0 using ASKAP's FLASH survey, reporting a new absorption detection and tentative stacked detections for associated galaxies.
AI.motivation: To probe the HI gas content of star-forming galaxies and radio galaxies at intermediate redshifts (0.4<z<1.0), where direct HI 21 cm emission detections are challenging, and to test whether background source optical depth limits and covering factors affect stacked HI 21 cm absorption detectability.
AI.method: HI 21 cm absorption search and stacking analysis using ASKAP's FLASH survey, targeting associated and intervening star-forming galaxies and radio galaxies at 0.4<z<1.0. Stacking was performed in order of descending radio source brightness, and meta-analysis of HI 21 cm surveys was used to validate detection expectations.
AI.result: A new HI 21 cm absorption detection in NVSS J214954-004657 at z=0.863. Tentative stacked detections for associated galaxies when stacked in descending radio brightness (buried as weaker sources are added). No stacked signal in intervening systems. No significant difference in detection rate between star-forming and general radio galaxies. One detection is consistent with expectations from survey meta-analysis.
AI.conclusion: Stacked HI 21 cm absorption detectability is governed by background source optical depth limits and covering factors, with covering factors more critical for intervening systems. Detection rates for associated absorption in star-forming galaxies are consistent with the general radio-source population at these redshifts.

title: GGI Lectures on Large-Scale Structure Perturbation Theory (Effective Field Theory)
comment: 87 pages, 19 figures, an extended version of lectures delivered at the "New Physics from Galaxy Clustering'' school at the Galileo Galilei Institute, Florence, in August 2025
summary: These notes are an introduction to non-linear perturbation theory for cosmological large-scale structure. They are aimed at undergraduate and beginning graduate students and do not require any cosmology or quantum field theory background. All necessary concepts are developed from scratch. The lectures are intended to explain all key ingredients needed to model the observed clustering of galaxies in real and redshift spaces. After a brief pedagogical introduction to the ideas of effective field theory (EFT), we develop large-scale structure EFT in the context of Newtonian cosmology using symmetry principles. We discuss in detail the shortcomings of Standard Perturbation Theory, the non-linear evolution of baryon acoustic oscillations and its relation to the equivalence principle, counterterms and renormalization of the loop diagrams, and stochastic effects. Then we develop EFT for galaxy bias and redshift space distortions. We also highlight some important facts about redshift-space stochasticity, relevant for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Finally, we introduce Lagrangian Perturbation Theory.

AI.tldr: Pedagogical lecture notes introducing non-linear perturbation theory for cosmological large-scale structure, targeting undergraduate and beginning graduate students with no prior cosmology or QFT background.
AI.motivation: Provide an accessible, self-contained introduction to non-linear perturbation theory for cosmological large-scale structure that requires no prior cosmology or quantum field theory background, aimed at undergraduate and beginning graduate students.
AI.method: Develops all necessary concepts from scratch, covering EFT in Newtonian cosmology using symmetry principles, shortcomings of Standard Perturbation Theory, non-linear evolution of BAOs, counterterms and loop renormalization, stochastic effects, EFT for galaxy bias and redshift space distortions, redshift-space stochasticity, and Lagrangian Perturbation Theory.
AI.result: A complete pedagogical framework covering key ingredients needed to model observed galaxy clustering in real and redshift spaces, from basic EFT ideas through to Lagrangian perturbation theory.
AI.conclusion: These lecture notes provide a comprehensive and accessible introduction to non-linear perturbation theory for large-scale structure, equipping students with the tools to model galaxy clustering in both real and redshift spaces.

title: Angular Momentum Evolution from Core to Disk Scales in the Early Phase of Star Formation: Constraints from HH 212, HH 211, and B335
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures
summary: I investigate the angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation using three protostellar systems: HH 212, HH 211, and B335. Observations show that the specific angular momentum follows a power-law dependence at core scales and transitions to an approximately constant value at smaller radii, indicating dynamical collapse in the inner envelope. I model this behavior using the inside-out collapse solution of Shu (1977) and its rotating extension, the Terebey-Shu-Cassen model, including modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. I find that the observed angular momentum profiles in all three sources are broadly consistent with an inside-out collapse scenario with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. The inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield total masses accreted onto the center that are broadly consistent with the central masses derived from kinematics, allowing for a fraction of the material to be ejected by jets and winds. The predicted midplane densities at typical radii, including the effect of magnetic flattening, are also consistent with observational estimates. The three systems exhibit a similar pattern of angular momentum evolution despite large differences in the magnitude of their specific angular momentum. In particular, the small disk in B335 can be naturally explained by its lower initial specific angular momentum, although alternative explanations, such as magnetic braking or different initial conditions, cannot be excluded. These results suggest that inside-out collapse, with modest magnetic modification, provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in the early phase of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales in early star formation across three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, and B335), showing that the inside-out collapse model (Shu 1977; Terebey-Shu-Cassen) with modest magnetic flattening broadly reproduces observed angular momentum profiles, collapse ages, accreted masses, and midplane densities.
AI.motivation: To understand how angular momentum is transported and evolves observationally from core scales to disk scales during the early phase of star formation, and to test whether canonical inside-out collapse models can account for the observed behavior across multiple protostellar systems.
AI.method: The author compares observed specific angular momentum profiles of three protostellar systems (HH 212, HH 211, B335) against theoretical predictions from the Shu (1977) inside-out collapse solution and its rotating extension (Terebey-Shu-Cassen model), modified to include modest magnetic effects through a flattened, magnetized core. Derived quantities (collapse ages, infall rates, accreted masses, midplane densities) are compared with kinematic and observational estimates.
AI.result: The observed angular momentum profiles in all three sources are broadly consistent with inside-out collapse with approximate conservation of specific angular momentum in the collapsing region. Inferred collapse ages and mass infall rates yield accreted total masses consistent with kinematic central masses (allowing for jet/wind ejection). Predicted midplane densities, including magnetic flattening effects, agree with observations. All three systems show a similar angular momentum evolution pattern despite large magnitude differences; the small disk in B335 is naturally explained by lower initial specific angular momentum, though magnetic braking or different initial conditions cannot be excluded.
AI.conclusion: Inside-out collapse with modest magnetic modification provides a plausible first-order description of angular momentum evolution from core to disk scales during the early phase of star formation.

title: Growth, geometry, and early-universe split of the matter density parameter $Ω_{\rm m}$
comment: 15 pages including references, 15 figures
summary: While the $Λ$ cold dark matter ($Λ$CDM) model can successfully reproduce the measurements of many cosmological probes, some discrepancies have recently emerged. Therefore, it is necessary to test the standard cosmological model for consistency. An important stress test is to separate the influence of different cosmological regimes on the parameter inference. We treat three regimes separately here: geometry, growth, and the early universe. The geometrical regime concerns the expansion and curvature history, while the growth regime governs structure formation and the early-universe regime affects physics prior to recombination. Previous analyses have performed the split between geometry and growth, whereas we also consider the early universe influence separately. We perform this split for the present day matter density parameter $Ω_{\rm m}$ using multiple cosmological observables. The used data are galaxy clustering and weak lensing statistics (3x2pt) from the Dark Energy Survey (DES), cosmic microwave background (CMB) data from Planck, spectroscopic baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), type-Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) samples from Pantheon+, and redshift-space distortions (RSD) from a collection of galaxy surveys. For each of these probes, we introduce a phenomenological split into these three regimes. This work shows a strong correlation between the geometric and the early regime for the matter density, but no strong correlation between the growth regime and the others. All regimes are compatible in the posterior distribution, however the difference between the geometry and the early regimes, $ΔΩ_{\rm m}^{\rm geo,early}$, is 2$σ$ apart from 0.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the ΛCDM model by splitting cosmological parameter inference into three regimes—geometry, growth, and early universe—and finds a strong correlation between the geometric and early regimes for the matter density parameter Ωm, but no strong correlation between growth and the others. All regimes are compatible in the posterior, though the difference ΔΩm^geo,early is ~2σ from zero, suggesting mild tension.
AI.motivation: The ΛCDM model faces emerging discrepancies from various cosmological probes. The authors aim to stress-test the standard model by independently assessing how different cosmological regimes (geometry, growth, early universe) influence parameter inference, going beyond previous geometry-growth splits to include the early-universe regime separately.
AI.method: The paper performs a three-way phenomenological split of the matter density parameter Ωm into geometric, growth, and early-universe regimes. It uses multiple cosmological datasets: DES galaxy clustering and weak lensing (3x2pt), Planck CMB data, DESI spectroscopic BAO, Pantheon+ SNe Ia, and RSD from galaxy surveys. For each probe, a phenomenological split across these three regimes is introduced, and posterior constraints on Ωm are derived.
AI.result: A strong correlation is found between the geometric and early-universe regimes for Ωm, while no strong correlation exists between the growth regime and the others. All regimes remain compatible within the posterior, but the difference between geometry and early regimes (ΔΩm^geo,early) is 2σ away from zero, indicating mild tension.
AI.conclusion: The three cosmological regimes are largely consistent within ΛCDM, but the ~2σ offset between geometry and early-universe inferred matter densities hints at possible tension, motivating further investigation into whether this indicates new physics or systematic effects.

title: Bipolar HII regions Produced by Cloud-Cloud Collisions
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We use numerical experiments to explore two possibilities: (i) that Bipolar H II Regions are the result of Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs), and (ii) that -- when allowance is made for the chaotic nature of such collisions, the short duration of the bipolar phase, and different viewing angles -- a large proportion of all H II Regions might be the aftermath of CCCs. To reduce the parameter space, our experiments only consider head-on collisions between two $500$ M$_\odot$ clouds, with three different levels of turbulence, and two different collision velocities; the collision velocities define the `collision axis'. In all experiments, OB stars only condense out after a Shock-Compressed Layer has formed (perpendicular to the collision axis), and fragmented to produce a Hub Filament System, with the OB stars forming in the Hub. Ionising radiation from the OB stars excites an H II Region, which tends to expand more rapidly in directions close to the collision axis, and more slowly in directions orthogonal to the collision axis, where it encounters the dense gas of the Shock-Compressed Layer. Consequently, the H II Region may appear bipolar, for a short period during its evolution, if observed at sufficiently large angle to the collision axis. Viewed from smaller angles, the waist appears as a Bright-Rim, similar to conventional approximately spherical H II Regions. Under this circumstance, there are other metrics -- based on the extent of diffuse freefree emission, the velocity dispersion of Radio Recombination Lines, dust emission at mid-infrared wavelengths -- that might indicate the aftermath of a CCC, and establish CCCs as a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: Using numerical simulations of head-on collisions between two 500 solar-mass clouds with varying turbulence and collision velocities, the paper explores whether Bipolar H II Regions result from Cloud-Cloud Collisions (CCCs) and whether most H II Regions may be the aftermath of CCCs. OB stars form in the Hub of a Shock-Compressed Layer, and the resulting H II Region appears bipolar only briefly and at specific viewing angles; otherwise it resembles a conventional spherical region but may show other CCC signatures (diffuse free-free emission, RRL velocity dispersion, mid-IR dust emission).
AI.motivation: To determine whether Cloud-Cloud Collisions are responsible for Bipolar H II Regions and, more broadly, whether CCCs could be a dominant trigger for high-mass star formation given the chaotic nature and short duration of the bipolar phase.
AI.method: Numerical experiments of head-on collisions between two 500 solar-mass clouds, varying turbulence levels (three) and collision velocities (two). The simulations track the formation of a Shock-Compressed Layer, its fragmentation into a Hub Filament System, OB star formation in the Hub, and subsequent H II region expansion under the influence of the anisotropic ambient density structure.
AI.result: The H II region expands faster along the collision axis and slower perpendicular to it (where dense shocked gas lies), producing a transient bipolar morphology visible only at large viewing angles relative to the collision axis. At smaller viewing angles it appears as a conventional spherical region with a Bright-Rim waist, and other diagnostic signatures (diffuse free-free emission, RRL velocity dispersion, mid-IR dust emission) may betray its CCC origin.
AI.conclusion: CCC-induced H II regions can appear bipolar only briefly and from specific viewing angles; however, alternative metrics may identify CCC aftermaths in apparently spherical regions, suggesting CCCs could be the dominant trigger for high-mass star formation.

title: Multi-branch classification of diffuse cluster radio emission
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, Accepted in A&A
summary: Context. Galaxy clusters sometimes host synchrotron radiation on scales of ~100 kpc to ~1 Mpc, with surface brightness only a few times the image noise. This diffuse cluster radio emission is a sensitive probe of magnetic fields and intracluster medium dynamics, but disentangling the underlying physical processes requires statistically large samples spanning a wide range of cluster masses, dynamical states, and redshifts, together with sufficient sensitivity to low-surface-brightness emission. Aims. We explore two techniques for improving detection of diffuse emission in galaxy cluster images, relative to a baseline classifier: the scattering transform (ST) and squeeze-excitation (SE) attention. Methods. We integrate an ST encoder into a dual-branch classifier (DualSSN) and a scattering network (ScatterNet). We incorporate SE attention into the DualSSN and dual-branch convolutional neural network (DualCSN). These classifiers are then benchmarked against a simple CNN, across ten image preprocessing configurations and three cropping strategies. Performance is evaluated on small labelled datasets from the second data release of the LOFAR two-metre sky survey overlapping with the second Planck catalogue of Sunyaev-Zel'dovich sources (LoTSS-DR2/PSZ2). Results. Alongside the multi-branch approach with SE and ST, cropping the image to a fixed number of telescope beams and uv- tapering (smoothing to a coarser angular resolution) improve classification performance, while stacking multiple preprocessed ver- sions of an image does not. Conclusions. Scattering-transform-based multi-branch architectures with beam-normalised cropping are a promising direction for diffuse emission classification in the SKA era.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates improved detection of diffuse radio emission in galaxy clusters using scattering transform (ST) and squeeze-excitation (SE) attention techniques integrated into multi-branch classifiers, benchmarked against a simple CNN on LOFAR survey data. Results show that multi-branch architectures with SE/ST, plus beam-normalised cropping and uv-tapering, improve classification performance, while image stacking does not.
AI.motivation: Diffuse cluster radio emission is a sensitive probe of magnetic fields and intracluster medium dynamics, but detecting it is challenging due to low surface brightness (only a few times image noise) and requires statistically large samples across wide ranges of cluster masses, dynamical states, and redshifts with sufficient sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors integrate an ST encoder into a dual-branch classifier (DualSSN) and a scattering network (ScatterNet), and incorporate SE attention into DualSSN and a dual-branch convolutional neural network (DualCSN). These are benchmarked against a simple CNN across ten image preprocessing configurations and three cropping strategies, using small labelled datasets from LoTSS-DR2/PSZ2.
AI.result: Multi-branch approaches with SE and ST, along with cropping images to a fixed number of telescope beams and uv-tapering (smoothing to coarser angular resolution), improve classification performance. Stacking multiple preprocessed versions of an image does not improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Scattering-transform-based multi-branch architectures with beam-normalised cropping represent a promising direction for diffuse emission classification in the SKA era.

title: Searching in HI for Massive Low Surface Brightness Galaxies: II. Completing the UGC Sample
summary: Although Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies are increasingly well studied, considerable uncertainty still exists as to both their range in properties and their evolutionary history. LSB galaxies provide a fascinating extreme in galaxy formation and evolution, allowing excellent tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories. Previously, our group successfully measured the HI gas and dynamical mass properties of 350 LSB galaxies, significantly increasing the number of known extreme LSB galaxies (massive, gas rich, etc.) in the process. Here we oresent 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations of a further 35 LBG galaxies, only two of which have previously published data. Of the 35, 19 were detected. This paper also includes the HI information for five additional galaxies detected accidentally (in the blank sky region or at alternative velocities), none of which has previously published HI results.

AI.tldr: This paper presents new 21-cm HI line observations of 35 Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies using the 100-m Green Bank Telescope, detecting 19 of them. Additionally, 5 galaxies were serendipitously detected in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities, none previously published. This work extends the authors' earlier survey of 350 LSB galaxies.
AI.motivation: LSB galaxies remain poorly understood in terms of their range of properties and evolutionary history. They provide extreme test cases for galaxy formation and evolution theories. The authors aim to expand the sample of LSB galaxies with measured HI gas and dynamical mass properties to better constrain theories.
AI.method: 100-m Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope 21-cm HI line observations were conducted on 35 LSB galaxies, only two of which had prior published data. Data were also collected for 5 additional serendipitous detections.
AI.result: 19 of the 35 targeted LSB galaxies were detected in HI. Five additional galaxies were detected accidentally (in blank sky regions or at alternative velocities), none of which had previously published HI data.
AI.conclusion: This study substantially increases the sample of LSB galaxies with measured HI properties, building on the prior survey of 350 LSB galaxies, and will enable better statistical characterization of these extreme galaxies and tests of galaxy formation and evolution theories.

title: Inflation, Open Universes, and Dark Energy
comment: 29 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables;
summary: We study the impact of spatial curvature ($Ω_k$) and dynamical dark energy (parametrized by $w_0$ and $w_a$) on the spectral index $n_s$ using a combination of cosmic microwave background datasets (Planck, SPT, and ACT), and spectroscopic galaxy samples from DESI, including both BAO and full-shape clustering measurements. We show that a small negative curvature, $Ω_k\simeq 3\times 10^{-3}$, lowers the value of $n_s$, bringing it closer to predictions of the Starobinsky, Higgs, and simplest $α$-attractor inflationary models. In particular, we find $n_s= 0.9667\pm0.0041$ (using Planck and DESI data) or $n_s= 0.9692\pm0.0035$ (adding ACT and SPT). Allowing for time-evolving dark energy also reduces the spectral index, leading to $n_s=0.9716\pm0.0032$ (from the combined dataset), or $n_s=0.9694\pm0.0035$ in combination with a small negative curvature. Our results demonstrate that the tension between current observational data and the Starobinsky, Higgs, and simplest $α$-attractor models holds only for $Λ$CDM, and can be mitigated in extended cosmological models. We discuss implications of these findings for inflationary models in an open universe and/or with dynamical dark energy, including scenarios with quantum tunneling and non-standard topology. Furthermore, we briefly describe a special class of $α$-attractor models, where one can make $n_s$ arbitrarily large, and we describe the $α$-attractor quintessence model. Such models may be of particular relevance when future data from DESI, as well as DESI-II, SPHEREx, Euclid, Rubin, and Roman, becomes available.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how spatial curvature (Ω_k) and dynamical dark energy (w0, wa) affect the inferred spectral index n_s. Using CMB data (Planck, SPT, ACT) combined with DESI galaxy clustering (BAO and full-shape), the authors find that small negative curvature (Ω_k≈3×10^-3) lowers n_s to 0.9667–0.9692, bringing it into better agreement with Starobinsky, Higgs, and simple α-attractor inflationary models. Dynamical dark energy also reduces n_s, and the combination of both extensions yields n_s≈0.9694. The tension between data and these inflationary models is shown to hold only under ΛCDM and can be mitigated in extended cosmologies. The paper also discusses implications for inflation in an open universe and α-attractor quintessence models, relevant for upcoming surveys.
AI.motivation: The spectral index n_s inferred from CMB and large-scale structure data under the standard ΛCDM model is in mild tension with predictions from well-motivated inflationary models such as Starobinsky, Higgs inflation, and α-attractors. The authors aim to test whether this tension persists when extending the cosmological model to include spatial curvature and dynamical dark energy, which are relatively poorly constrained by current data.
AI.method: The analysis combines CMB datasets (Planck, SPT, ACT) with spectroscopic galaxy samples from DESI, using both BAO and full-shape clustering measurements. The parameter space includes Ω_k (spatial curvature) and (w0, wa) (dynamical dark energy parametrization), alongside the standard cosmological parameters. Constraints on n_s are derived under various model configurations, including ΛCDM, open ΛCDM, w0wa CDM, and combinations thereof.
AI.result: Small negative curvature lowers n_s to 0.9667±0.0041 (Planck+DESI) or 0.9692±0.0035 (adding ACT and SPT). Dynamical dark energy alone yields n_s=0.9716±0.0032, and combined with curvature gives n_s=0.9694±0.0035. These values are closer to inflationary model predictions than the ΛCDM value, demonstrating that the tension is mitigated in extended models.
AI.conclusion: The tension between observational data and Starobinsky/Higgs/α-attractor inflationary models is not robust under model extensions: both spatial curvature and dynamical dark energy can alleviate it. The authors discuss implications for inflation in an open universe, including quantum tunneling and non-standard topology scenarios, and highlight α-attractor quintessence models as potentially relevant for future surveys (DESI-II, SPHEREx, Euclid, Rubin, Roman).

title: JWST's Constraints on the Substellar IMF in NGC 2024
comment: MNRAS, in press
summary: A recent study has reported the detection of a turnover in the initial mass function (IMF) below 12 Mjup and the possible detection of a minimum mass near 3 Mjup in the heavily embedded cluster NGC 2024 (<1 Myr), which was based on a sample of brown dwarf candidates in NIRCam images from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). I have used those NIRCam data in conjunction with archival spectra from JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) to constrain the substellar IMF in NGC 2024. I present NIRSpec data for 87 sources, 67 of which are within the NIRCam field. Based on those spectra and data from previous studies (e.g., X-ray emission), I have classified 45 of the NIRSpec targets as members of NGC 2024, 17 of which have spectral types indicative of brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 are within NIRCam). The latter have mass estimates as low as 4 Mjup according to theoretical evolutionary models. There remain a few photometric candidates lacking spectra that extend down to the completeness limit of the images (>=2 Mjup for Ak>=1), so the minimum mass of the IMF has not been detected. It is not possible to measure a reliable substellar IMF from the NIRCam images because of the small number of brown dwarfs encompassed by them, a bias against objects at lower masses due to the high extinctions, and incompleteness at >=10 Mjup due to the saturation limit. Thus, there is no evidence in the JWST data for a turnover below 12jup.

AI.tldr: The author re-examines the substellar initial mass function (IMF) in NGC 2024 using JWST NIRSpec spectra for 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field), classifying 45 as cluster members and identifying 17 brown dwarfs (M6.5-L) with masses down to ~4 Mjup. The author finds no evidence for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup or a minimum mass near 3 Mjup, as the NIRCam data suffer from small brown dwarf sample sizes, extinction bias, and saturation incompleteness.
AI.motivation: A prior study claimed the detection of an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup and a possible minimum mass near 3 Mjup in NGC 2024, based on NIRCam photometric brown dwarf candidates. This work seeks to test those claims with follow-up NIRSpec spectroscopy in the same cluster.
AI.method: The author combined JWST NIRCam photometry with archival JWST NIRSpec spectra of 87 sources (67 within the NIRCam field). Membership was determined using spectra plus prior X-ray data, and spectral types were used to derive masses via theoretical evolutionary models.
AI.result: 45 NIRSpec targets were classified as NGC 2024 members, 17 of which are brown dwarfs (M6.5-L; 13 within NIRCam), with masses as low as ~4 Mjup. However, photometric candidates without spectra extend to ~2 Mjup, so the minimum IMF mass is not detected. The substellar IMF cannot be reliably measured from NIRCam data due to small brown dwarf numbers, extinction-biased lower masses, and saturation-limited incompleteness at >=10 Mjup.
AI.conclusion: There is no evidence in the JWST data for an IMF turnover below 12 Mjup in NGC 2024; the previously reported turnover and minimum mass are not supported by spectroscopic follow-up.

title: Beyond monomial $α$-attractors
comment: Comments welcome!
summary: Recent small-scale CMB data show a preference for larger scalar spectral index, $n_s$, when combined with DESI data. Monomial $α$-attractor T-models can be reconciled with the new observations if the power of the hyperbolic tangent function is $p\geq 6$, where $p$ is even. The supergravity construction of monomial T-models with $p>2$ relies on the assumption that lower powers remain negligible over the whole field range explored during inflation and reheating. What would be the consequences of going beyond the monomial formulation? As a first step in this direction, we consider the case of a binomial potential, given by the sum of quadratic and quartic terms. title: X-ray Absorption Variability in NGC 1142: Another Constraint on the Nature of the Torus/Broad-Line Region in Active Galactic Nuclei
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The physics, geometry, and kinematics of the gas and dust surrounding the central engine of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are not well understood. We use the physically-motivated torus models UXCLUMPY, XSKIRTor, and RXTorusD to model the spectra. Our results confirm the previously observed trends, and we compare these trends to simulated obscuration curves assuming different locations and distributions of obscuring clouds.

title: Dark Matter Constraints from Small-Scale Cosmic Structure
comment: 73 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables; submitted to Reviews of Modern Physics; comments welcome
summary: Small-scale cosmic structure provides a powerful test of the fundamental nature of dark matter (DM). A wide range of DM models impact matter clustering on small scales, including warm, fuzzy, and (self-)interacting DM. In these scenarios, DM physics such as free-streaming, wave interference, and self/Standard Model interactions alter the abundance and internal structure of DM halos. Cosmological and astrophysical probes of nonlinear structure---including dwarf galaxies, strong lensing, the Lyman-$α$ forest, stellar streams, and high-redshift galaxies---are therefore sensitive to these effects. Here, we review DM constraints provided by small-scale structure, focusing on observables that probe scales smaller than $\sim 1~\mathrm{Mpc}$, which define the frontier of current measurements. We summarize how these constraints have been translated to limits on microphysical DM models, and we discuss key modeling uncertainties and observational systematics. Finally, we highlight the growing importance of probe combination and simulation-based inference for this field, and we overview upcoming observational facilities that will sharpen small-scale structure tests of DM physics.

It also summarizes the translation of these constraints into limits on microphysical DM parameters, discusses modeling uncertainties and observational systematics, and highlights the growing role of probe combination, simulation-based inference, and upcoming observational facilities.

title: Characterizing the disruption of Böotes III: a missing link in the Galactic halo?
comment: 27 pages, 16 figures; Submitted to ApJ
summary: The Böotes III (Boo3) dwarf galaxy has long been suspected of being the progenitor of Styx, a ~50°-long stellar stream that was simultaneously discovered in the same region of sky. Boo3's diffuse morphology, large velocity dispersion, small pericenter, and excess of candidate stars at large radii suggest it is undergoing active tidal disruption. Here, we re-examine the Boo3-Styx association by searching for Boo3's tidal debris using a combination of Gaia-selected members, new CaHK narrow-band imaging with CFHT/MegaCam, and stellar tracer catalogues of blue horizontal branch and red giant branch stars. Despite our extensive search, we find no observational evidence directly linking Boo3 to Styx. Furthermore, our results suggest that either Boo3's extended substructure is too diffuse to be detected with current data, or that its particular orbit may have erased a coherent tidal signature. Boo3 thus remains an enigmatic system, and exemplifies the need for spectroscopic follow-up to properly disentangle the nature between this faint Milky Way satellite and nearby stream.

title: Axion Inflation with a Massive Abelian Gauge Field
comment: 52 pages, 11 figures, 1 table, 5 appendices
summary: An axial coupling between an inflaton and an Abelian gauge field can trigger the tachyonic amplification of one gauge-field helicity. For a massless vector, modes with physical momentum $k/a\sim |ξ|H$ are enhanced by approximately $\exp(π|ξ|)$, and sufficiently efficient production can provide substantial friction for the homogeneous inflaton. We extend this mechanism to a vector of mass $m$. The instability is present only for $|ξ|>\bar m\equiv m/H$, and in the heavy regime the mode amplitude scales as $\exp[π(|ξ|-\bar m)]$. Because the amplified modes remain well inside the Hubble radius when $\bar m\gg1$, their contribution to long-wavelength curvature perturbations is power-law suppressed at fixed background backreaction. In the weak-backreaction regime we obtain ${\cal P}^{\rm id}_ζ \propto \bar m^{-2}$, while including the gauge-induced friction of scalar perturbations gives the scaling ${\cal P}^{\rm id}_ζ\propto \bar{m}^{-3}$. These estimates indicate that ${\cal P}^{\rm id}_ζ\lesssim 10^{-9}$ on CMB scales should be compatible with gauge field backreaction for $\bar{m}$ larger than order a few hundred. We test the analytical mode functions and backreaction estimates with the first lattice simulations based on a massive-vector extension of the \texttt{Pencil Code}, including simulations in the strongly backreacting regime.

The heavy-mass regime suppresses contributions to curvature perturbations, scaling as m̄^(-2) or m̄^(-3) depending on the backreaction treatment, allowing P_ζ ≲ 10^(-9) on CMB scales for m̄ ≳ few hundred. The analytical predictions are validated with the first lattice simulations of a massive-vector Pencil Code extension.

title: Cosmo-SPINN: Fuzzy Dark Matter Simulations with Physics-Informed Generative Networks
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures (2 more in Appendix), submitted to ApJ; comments welcome
summary: Generative machine learning models have recently emerged as powerful tools for producing cosmological simulations. However, many existing emulators do not explicitly enforce the underlying physical dynamics governing cosmological evolution, often leading to artifacts and poor adherence to the evolution equations. In this work, we present a physics-informed generative U-Net framework for fuzzy dark matter (FDM) that addresses two complementary tasks: (i) the evolution of cosmological fields from initial conditions to an arbitrary cosmological scale factor and (ii) the super-resolution of FDM simulations at a specified cosmological scale factor. Our model incorporates a physics-informed loss function that explicitly enforces consistency with the underlying Schrödinger-Poisson (SP) dynamics during training. For the evolution task, we find that the inclusion of this physics-based loss significantly improves the quality of the predicted simulations, even when only a small amount of training data is available. Using only 20% of the training data, the model accurately reproduces the target simulations in a 1 $h^{-1}$ Mpc box. Furthermore, the framework generalizes effectively across previously unseen realizations of the initial conditions. For the super-resolution task, we present, for the first time, a generative super-resolution model trained on FDM simulations obtained by solving the full SP equations, considering both single and multiple realizations of the initial conditions and analyzing the role of the physics-informed loss in each case. Our approach enables modern generative modeling of cosmological simulations while maintaining physical consistency and substantially reducing generative artifacts.
